en: You can observe Mayon Volcano in Albay from Legazpi City because its frequent eruptions have built a near-perfect, symmetrical conical shape.
The lower half of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan is tidal, meaning you can observe the water level rising and falling with the sea.
You can observe the giant Rafflesia flower in Mount Banahaw, which blooms with a massive red body and emits a foul smell to attract flies.
You can observe the amihan season from November to February when cool northeast monsoon winds bring dry weather and clear skies to the Philippines.
You can observe Taal Lake in Batangas as a large freshwater body that completely surrounds Volcano Island, which itself holds a smaller crater lake.
Hikers near the summit of Mount Pulag can observe a mossy forest, where frequent thick fog and cold temperatures cover the trees in damp green moss.
You can observe the over 1,200 symmetrical mounds of the Chocolate Hills in Bohol turn brown during the dry season because the grass loses moisture.
You can observe the twin drops of Maria Cristina Falls in Lanao del Norte plunging down a high cliff, which generates hydroelectric power for Mindanao.
You can observe the Philippine tarsier in Bohol sanctuaries using its exceptionally large eyes to spot and hunt small insects in the dark forests.
You can observe the pink sand beach of Great Santa Cruz Island, which is created by crushed red organ pipe coral mixing with white sand.
You can observe the above-ground roots of mangrove trees in Zamboanga Sibugay, which act like snorkels to help the plants breathe in muddy, oxygen-poor soil.
Inside Sumaging Cave in Sagada, you can observe large stalactites and stalagmites that slowly form from the constant dripping of mineral-rich water over thousands of years.
